what: Micro-frontends split a large web app into independently built and deployed pieces, owned by different teams, that a host (container) app composes into one page at runtime. Module Federation is a popular way to do this: each build exposes modules and the host loads them from remote URLs when needed.
like: Like a shopping mall: each shop is run by its own team and can refit its shop overnight, while the mall provides the entrance, signs and shared corridors.
why: Teams ship on their own schedule without waiting for a big release
Large apps can be upgraded or rewritten piece by piece
Clear ownership: each team owns a vertical slice end to end

nodes.t: Remote A: Catalog|own repo and deploy
Remote B: Checkout|own repo and deploy

steps.d: Each team owns a vertical slice - say catalog, checkout, account - with its own repo, pipeline and release. Martin Fowler describes teams owning vertical slices of functionality, often one page each, from idea to production.
The host owns the layout, routing and authentication. It lists remotes as name@url and loads a remote's entry script only when its route is opened.
A remote declares what it exposes (keys start with ./, such as ./Button). The host imports app1/Button as a normal async import. Loading is always asynchronous.
Both sides register React in a share scope. Without singleton set, each side may load its own copy. Singleton makes the higher version win and warns the lower side.
A team publishes new chunks and a new remote entry; the host picks them up on next load without being rebuilt. Contracts - routes, events, props - must stay backwards compatible.

numbers.l: default of Module Federation's singleton option, so each side loads its own copy of a shared library unless you turn it on
to use a remote module: load it asynchronously, then evaluate it; remotes can never be used without a chunk load
to integrate micro-frontends in Fowler's article: server-side templates, build-time packages, iframes, JavaScript and Web Components

choices.t: Do you need it at all
choices.d: It solves an organisation problem - many teams, one product - not a technical one. For one or two teams a modular monolith in a monorepo is simpler and lighter.

Run-time JavaScript or Module Federation is the usual default. Iframes give the strongest isolation at the cost of routing, deep linking and responsiveness. Build-time packaging forces lockstep releases and is advised against.
Sharing React as a singleton avoids duplicate downloads and two Reacts on one page, but ties teams to compatible version ranges. Mismatches log warnings and can break.
Isolate CSS with naming conventions, CSS modules or Shadow DOM, and share only generic primitives through a design system, not domain logic.

instead.why: One consistent UI across teams without separate deployments
A monorepo with route-level code splitting is often enough

breaks.d: Remotes bundle their own copy or share incompatible versions.
breaks.see: Hook errors, larger downloads, console warnings about versions
breaks.fix: Configure shared with singleton and a requiredVersion range; set a unique name for each build

breaks.d: A remote's URL fails or a new release changes an exposed module.
breaks.see: Blank region or crash in the host
breaks.fix: Error boundary and fallback UI around each remote, versioned contracts, canary rollout

breaks.d: Each team solves styling its own way.
breaks.fix: Shared design system and tokens, CSS scoping, regular integration in a production-like environment

say: I would only reach for micro-frontends when several teams need to release independently; the host owns shell, routing and auth, and each team ships a vertical slice.
With Module Federation the host loads remote entries at runtime, and I share React as a singleton while giving each build a unique name and wrapping every remote in an error boundary.
Shared UI comes from a design system, and the contracts between slices - routes, events, props - are versioned and tested so teams can deploy without coordination.

followups.a: Keep it minimal: custom events, props from the host, or the URL. Treat routes and message formats as contracts and verify them with contract tests.
Payload size and operational complexity: duplicated dependencies, more pipelines and domains, and consistency between teams all need strong automation and governance.

today: Module Federation 2.0 adds a manifest, a runtime and a plugin system, works with Webpack and Rspack, and lists DevTools, router and SSR support on its roadmap; Vercel also offers a microfrontends configuration at the platform level.

check.q: What is the main reason to adopt micro-frontends?
check.why: It is an organisational scaling pattern; bundle size can get worse.

check.q: Without singleton enabled, two builds with different React versions will...
check.why: singleton defaults to false, so versions are not forced into one.

check.q: Which integration approach does Fowler advise against?
check.why: Publishing each piece as a package forces lockstep releases and defeats independence.
